name: Whitening toothpaste
lead: Whitening toothpaste is toothpaste marketed to make teeth look lighter, using mild abrasives, chemical stain-loosening agents, in some products peroxide, or optical agents such as blue covarine [1][2]. It is widely sold over the counter as a low-cost alternative to professional bleaching.

Research and reference sources generally describe the effect as removal or masking of surface (extrinsic) stains rather than a change in the natural tooth colour. Wikipedia reports that daily use typically takes two to four weeks to produce visible lightening and that a 2017 systematic review found nearly all whitening dentifrices reduced extrinsic stain [1]. A 2025 randomised crossover trial examined blue covarine toothpastes and tooth colour [3].
infobox: Abrasion, stain-loosening agents, peroxide, optical agents [1][2]

paras: Abrasion is the main way any toothpaste removes stain, and whitening formulas may add polishing agents to lift it more effectively [1]. Some contain peroxide, the ingredient found in bleaching gels, while others use additives such as sodium tripolyphosphate to loosen stain [1]. Blue covarine products deposit a blue pigment intended to shift the apparent colour of the tooth surface [3].

Toothpaste is reported to remove surface stains only and not to reverse discolouration from within the tooth [1]. A review of natural whitening approaches states that stains from tea, coffee, tobacco, food dyes and antibiotics such as tetracycline contribute to discolouration and that high-concentration peroxide whiteners can demineralise teeth if used excessively [2]. An in situ randomised study compared the whitening effect of different toothpastes on bovine enamel [4].

Abrasive toothpastes are rated by relative dentin abrasivity; a value below 250 is considered safe for lifelong use by ANSI and the ADA according to Wikipedia, and values above that may damage tooth surfaces [1]. Excessive use is described as potentially harmful to enamel [1]. A Cochrane review separately examines fluoride toothpaste for caries prevention [5], and a 18-month trial compared a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste with 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste in adults [6].

Discussion on looksmax.org touches on toothpaste mainly through fluoride safety: one thread debated whether fluoride-free "natural" toothpaste gives any protection against decay, with a poster arguing that dentists dissuade patients from fluoride-free products [7].

Randomised studies include a crossover trial of blue covarine toothpastes and tooth colour [3] and an in situ trial of whitening toothpastes on bovine enamel [4]. Abstract details were not available for these in the sources reviewed, so their effect sizes are not reported here. Large trials of toothpaste more broadly concern caries prevention rather than whitening [5][6].

lore.intro: Toothpaste appears in looksmax.org mostly in discussions of fluoride safety rather than whitening [7].

claims.claim: Fluoride-free toothpaste is safe and just as good, or fluoride is harmful
claims.believers: Some posters question fluoride and prefer natural products, while others reply that the natural versions mainly give a fresher mouth [7].
claims.experts: A Cochrane network meta-analysis examined fluoride toothpastes of different concentrations for preventing caries [5]; a trial found a hydroxyapatite toothpaste non-inferior to fluoride in adults over 18 months [6].

card.summary: Everyday toothpaste with stain-lifting extras: it lightens surface stain in weeks, not the tooth's natural shade.
card.note: Highly abrasive formulas can wear enamel; effect stops when use stops.

quick.overview:
Whitening toothpaste uses polishing agents, stain-loosening chemicals, sometimes peroxide or a blue pigment, to make teeth look lighter.

A systematic review cited by Wikipedia found nearly all such products reduce surface stain, but they do not change the natural colour of the tooth.
quick.mechanism: Mostly mechanical and chemical removal of surface stains, with some products adding peroxide or optical pigments.
quick.risks: Abrasivity (measured as RDA) can wear enamel with excessive use; peroxide products can demineralise teeth at high concentrations.
